entries.title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
entries.summary: Coding agents work in tasks, and the number that matters is cost per solved task, not price per token. In this post, you use the AWS CDK to deploy LiteLLM with the NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard routing plugin on Amazon Bedrock, then measure cost per solved task for a routed model group against single-model baselines.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard

Coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI work in tasks. A developer asks for a change, and the agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests until the work is done. One task can take a few model calls or dozens. What the developer pays for is the task, not one call.

The price per token alone doesn’t tell you what a whole task costs. The total depends on how many turns a model needs, how much history each turn replays, and how often a task has to be retried or never finishes. You pay for every attempt, including attempts on tasks that never finish. So when you route a coding agent’s requests between models, judge the routing by cost per solved task: the total cost of your runs divided by the number of runs whose tests pass.

NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard is an open source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. You define the models that it can use and the strategy that it follows. Its LiteLLM integration supports two strategies. Stage routing reads the recent tool activity and results in the request history, and then picks one of two candidate models. Random routing picks from the configured models, with optional weights, for traffic splits and A/B comparisons. Another option you can explore is LiteLLM, who also recently shipped a native built-in Switchyard stage router as an auto-router strategy.

In this post, you use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy LiteLLM, an open source gateway for large language models (LLMs), with the Switchyard routing plugin in your AWS account. LiteLLM calls the models on Amazon Bedrock. You then use the sample’s benchmark runners to measure cost per solved task for a routed model group and for single-model baseline groups, so that you can evaluate routing against your own workloads.

Note: The sample installs 

switchyard-server
0.3.0 from crates.io and runs the published LiteLLM v1.102.0 image. NVIDIA documents 
switchyard-server
0.3.0 as a demo and evaluation component, and its configuration can change between releases. This sample uses the experimental Switchyard LiteLLM integration and its configuration and APIs may change between releases. This is sample code, for non-production usage. Work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before deployment. Deploy the sample in a non-production account and test it before relying on it.

Solution overview

Figure 1 shows the architecture of the solution. LiteLLM and the Switchyard plugin run in one container image on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate, in private subnets.

A request flows through these steps. The numbers match the diagram.

  • The coding agent sends an OpenAI-compatible request with the model field set to 
    switchyard
    , the LiteLLM model group that Switchyard routes, and the shared gateway key in the 
    Authorization
    header. The endpoint is your hostname over HTTPS, with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate on the load balancer, and only the IPv4 CIDR range that you allow can reach it. With a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53, Route 53 resolves the hostname to the load balancer.
  • AWS WAF filters the request with IP reputation, known bad input, and per-IP rate-limit rules. The Application Load Balancer forwards only 
    /v1/chat/completions
    , 
    /v1/models
    , and 
    /health/liveliness
    to the ECS task in a private subnet, and answers every other path with 404.
  • The task runs one container: LiteLLM with the embedded Switchyard plugin. LiteLLM validates the gateway key and calls the plugin to pick a model. Stage chooses between a capable model and a lower-cost efficient model. It reads the tool activity and results in the request history, so the agent must send the full conversation history. Random chooses from a weighted pool. Neither strategy calls a judge model.
  • LiteLLM calls the selected model through the Amazon Bedrock 
    Converse
    or 
    ConverseStream
    API, with the task’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for credentials. The call goes through an Amazon Bedrock Runtime interface endpoint in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), so inference traffic stays on the AWS network.
  • The response or token stream returns through LiteLLM and the load balancer. The 
    x-litellm-model-name
    response header names the model that answered. The response body’s 
    model
    field stays 
    switchyard
    .

LiteLLM listens on port 4000 in the container and is the load balancer’s target, and the task’s security group admits only the load balancer. The path allowlist keeps the LiteLLM admin UI, API docs, and key management routes unreachable. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) holds the gateway image. AWS Secrets Manager generates the secret behind the gateway key, and the container adds the 

sk-
prefix when it starts. The task definition passes the profile files in 
LITELLM_CONFIG_TEXT
and 
SWITCHYARD_CONFIG_TEXT
, and the startup script writes them to 
/tmp
before it starts LiteLLM. Logs go to one Amazon CloudWatch log group, 
//litellm
, which keeps them for 30 days, and Container Insights collects metrics. The VPC spans two Availability Zones, and one NAT gateway provides outbound access for image pulls and other AWS services.

The plugin supports Stage routing, which needs exactly two candidates, and Random routing, which needs at least two and splits traffic by weight for A/B tests. Classifier-backed strategies, such as Task and Composite routing, need intermediate model calls that this integration doesn’t support. See the Switchyard routing overview for the full catalog.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need the following:

  • A non-production AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access to Claude Opus 5.5 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super 120B. The pair has been tested in US East (N. Virginia). For other AWS Regions, check Regional availability by models and tool-calling support.
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 with configured credentials and an explicit AWS Region, in an account and Region that are bootstrapped for the AWS CDK.
  • Node.js 20 or later, npm, Docker with BuildKit, and Python 3.11 or later.
  • A hostname that you own, with either a public Route 53 hosted zone for its domain or an ACM certificate for it in the deployment Region. A short plain-HTTP test needs neither.

Walkthrough

You define the model group, configure Stage, deploy and test the gateway, and measure cost. Start by cloning the sample repository:

Step 1: Define the model group in LiteLLM

A LiteLLM model group is one public model name with one or more deployments behind it. The sample keeps its configuration in deployment profiles under 

profiles/
. Each profile pairs 
litellm.yaml
, which defines the models and gateway settings, with 
switchyard.toml
, which controls how Switchyard picks a model. The following excerpt of 
profiles/stage/litellm.yaml
defines the routed 
switchyard
group, two single-model baseline groups, and the plugin registration:

Both candidates share 

model_name: switchyard
, so your client sends 
"model": "switchyard"
and Switchyard picks a candidate. List the capable model first and the efficient model second, because Stage reads the roles from that order.

The 

claude-opus-5-5
and 
nemotron-super-3-120b
groups are single-model baselines. Each one always answers with its own model, so you can compare the routed group’s cost and pass rate with each model alone in the same deployment. The Stage plugin alone rejects a group without two candidates, so the image registers a small wrapper, 
switchyard_gateway.configured.ROUTING_PLUGIN
. It applies Switchyard to groups with two or more unique candidates and passes single-model groups through. The configuration registers the wrapper twice: to pick the model and to apply the request changes that Switchyard records.

Every model uses 

bedrock/converse/
, so every candidate goes through the Amazon Bedrock 
Converse
API, and validation rejects any other route. The LiteLLM 
request_timeout
of 600 seconds matches the load balancer’s 10-minute idle timeout.

The file holds no credentials. LiteLLM reads the gateway key from the environment, and the task role supplies the AWS credentials. Never add credentials such as 

aws_access_key_id
, 
aws_secret_access_key
, or 
api_key
under 
litellm_params
: the stack copies the whole 
litellm.yaml
into the task definition and the AWS CloudFormation template in plain text.

The stack derives the task role’s Amazon Bedrock permissions from this file. For a global cross-Region inference profile, the foundation-model resource uses a 

*
Region and a trailing 
*
, so it also matches other model IDs with the same prefix. Review the derived policy before you deploy.

The 

global.
prefix marks a global cross-Region inference profile, and Amazon Bedrock might process those requests in supported commercial AWS Regions worldwide. If processing location matters, use a geographic profile or an in-Region model ID instead. For Nemotron 3 Super, the profile uses the in-Region model ID 
nvidia.nemotron-super-3-120b
, which you can switch for any model for testing.

Step 2: Configure Stage routing

Switchyard reads its algorithm and settings from 

switchyard.toml
. The default profile, 
profiles/stage/switchyard.toml
, configures Stage:

The settings work as follows:

  • picker = "efficient_first"
    : Stage uses the efficient model when the signals in the history are inconclusive. A new request has no tool results yet, so it goes to Nemotron 3 Super.
  • confidence_threshold
    : the confidence cutoff for the execution signals that Stage scores, from 0 through 1.
  • recent_window = 3
    : Stage examines the three most recent tool results.
  • only_on_wrong_signal_escalation = true
    : the Switchyard default. It controls when Stage adds an optional escalation note, and this profile sets no note.

Stage also accepts optional handoff notes and per-tier system prompts (

escalation_note
, 
deescalation_note
, 
capable_system_prompt
, and 
efficient_system_prompt
). The sample profile sets none of them.

For an A/B test, the Random profile in 

profiles/random/
uses the same models with 
algorithm = "random"
and 
weights = [0.5, 0.5]
, one weight per unique candidate in declaration order. To deploy it, add 
-c routingProfile=random
to the 
cdk diff
and 
cdk deploy
commands in Step 3.

The stack validates both files together when it synthesizes, and the preflight script runs the same checks. To check a profile change on its own, without AWS calls, run 

npm run validate:profile -- stage
. Invalid settings stop LiteLLM when it starts, and unsupported message shapes fail before inference.

Optional: Run the gateway locally

You can try the gateway on your machine before you deploy anything. Docker Compose builds the same image and reads the same profile files that the stack deploys to Amazon ECS. Run from the repository root:

The key that you export takes precedence over the placeholder in 

.env
, so Compose and the smoke test use the same one. AWS credentials come only from your shell and never go in 
.env
or the profile files. Compose publishes the gateway on 
127.0.0.1
only. There’s no load balancer locally, so the smoke test skips its closed-path checks. The local gateway still calls Amazon Bedrock, and those calls are billed. When you’re finished, run 
docker compose down
.

Step 3: Deploy the gateway

The gateway serves HTTPS on a hostname that you own. Set 

GATEWAY_DOMAIN
to that hostname and 
HOSTED_ZONE
to an existing Route 53 public hosted zone that contains it. The AWS CDK then creates a DNS-validated ACM certificate and the alias record. From the repository root, install the dependencies, run the read-only preflight check, and deploy:

If your domain’s DNS isn’t in Route 53, use an existing ACM certificate instead. Set 

CERTIFICATE_ARN
to an ACM certificate for the hostname in the deployment Region, and replace 
-c hostedZone="$HOSTED_ZONE"
with 
-c certificateArn="$CERTIFICATE_ARN"
in both commands. The AWS CDK then creates no certificate and no DNS record. After the deployment, create a CNAME record (or a Route 53 alias) that points the hostname at the 
LoadBalancerDnsName
output.

The required 

allowedCidr
value limits which networks can reach the load balancer, and the command sets it to your current public IPv4 address. Keep it to your own 
/32
: everyone who shares an allowed address, such as an office NAT or a VPN exit, can reach the endpoint. The stack refuses to synthesize without 
allowedCidr
, with a world-open range such as 
0.0.0.0/0
, or with an IPv6 range.

Preflight checks the configuration, your tools, and your AWS access, including access to each model in the profile, without making inference requests. The AWS CDK builds the gateway image, publishes it to Amazon ECR, and deploys the stack. Deployment prints these outputs:

OutputWhat it is
GatewayUrlThe base URL. The OpenAI-compatible API is under 
/v1
.
MasterKeySecretArnThe Secrets Manager secret behind the gateway key. The full key is 
sk-
followed by the secret value.
MasterKeyCommandA command that prints the gateway key.
SmokeTestCommandThe smoke test command, with the stack name, Region, and profile filled in.
RoutingProfileThe active routing profile, stage by default.
ClusterName, ServiceNameThe ECS cluster and service. The key rotation steps use them.
LoadBalancerDnsNameOnly with certificateArn: the name to point your hostname at.

Always give clients the 

https://
URL. Port 80 stays open only to redirect to HTTPS, and a client configured with 
http://
has already sent the key and its first request in clear text when the redirect arrives.

The load balancer idle timeout is 10 minutes, for long agent responses. The web ACL uses the Amazon IP reputation list and the known bad inputs rule group. It also limits each IP address to 2,000 requests per 5 minutes. It leaves out the generic body rules for cross-site scripting, SQL injection, and body size, which the source code in agent requests triggers. The 

allowedCidr
range and the gateway key still apply.

Quick test over plain HTTP. Without HTTPS settings, synth stops with an error. For a short test without a domain, you can opt in to plain HTTP on the load balancer’s DNS name:

With 

allowPlainHttp=true
, the AWS CDK prints a warning every time it synthesizes the stack. The gateway key in the 
Authorization
header, your prompts, the tool results and source code that your agent sends, and the model responses cross the network unencrypted between your client and the load balancer. Use the opt-in only for a short test with non-sensitive code from your own 
/32
. Then rotate the key, and run 
cdk destroy
when you finish. To move the same stack to HTTPS later, deploy it again with the HTTPS settings and without 
allowPlainHttp
.

Step 4: Test the gateway

In the same terminal that you used for the deployment, read the AWS CloudFormation stack outputs and build the gateway key:

Send a request to the 

switchyard
model group:

Look for HTTP 200 and a response. The 

x-litellm-model-name
response header shows the selected model as the full LiteLLM model string. A new request has no tool results to score, so Stage picks the efficient model, 
bedrock/converse/nvidia.nemotron-super-3-120b
.

To check health, authentication, and routing, run the smoke test:

The smoke test checks the health endpoint, that closed paths such as 

/ui
get the load balancer’s own 404, that a request without a key gets 401, and that 
/v1/models
lists every model group. For Stage, it checks that an ordinary request selects the efficient model and that a recorded history of repeated failures escalates to the capable model. Then it sends one request to each baseline group. The request and the smoke test make billable Amazon Bedrock calls.

To try your own agent, use 

$GATEWAY_URL/v1
as its OpenAI-compatible base URL, the gateway key as its API key, and 
switchyard
as the model. Stage needs the full supported request history with every request. The upstream adapter supports text messages, function tool calls, and text tool results, and unsupported message shapes fail before inference. The load balancer forwards the Chat Completions path but not the OpenAI Responses or Anthropic Messages paths. Clients that use those APIs get a 404 until you add the path, test it against the local container, and redeploy.

Step 5: Measure cost per solved task

The sample’s coding runner, 

bench/run.py
, lets a small coding agent list and read files, replace source files, and run the supplied unit tests through the gateway. A task is solved when its tests pass at the end, within six model turns by default. List the tasks and start with 
slugify
on the routed group:

The terminal shows the task, the selected models, the tool actions, the test results, and the final code diff. Each run saves its starting files, final workspace, transcript, patch, and result under 

bench/results/
.
TaskWhat the agent must do
slugifyFix a short function that builds URL slugs.
romanWrite a function that converts integers to Roman numerals.
calcWrite an expression parser without 
eval
, with precedence, a power operator, functions, and error handling.
lru_ttlWrite a thread-safe least recently used (LRU) cache with per-entry expiry and exact counters.

To give the arithmetic parser task room to run tests and attempt repairs, raise the turn limit:

After the runs, the runner prints one row per model group, with RUNS, SOLVED, ERRORS, COST/TASK, and COST/SOLVED columns. Cost per solved task is the estimated cost of all runs on a group divided by the runs whose tests passed. The runner prices each turn from the model in its 

x-litellm-model-name
header and the token usage in the response, using the PRICES table in 
bench/run.py
. A turn with cached input, a model without a PRICES entry, or a response without the header or token counts stays unpriced instead of counting as zero. Add a PRICES entry when you add a model to a profile, and check Amazon Bedrock pricing for current prices. A few runs on two tasks demonstrate the workflow. They aren’t enough to draw conclusions about cost or quality.

A group shows n/a with the reason when any of its runs is unpriced, and COST/SOLVED shows 

-
when no run was solved. To see where the cost went, check the turns: the terminal prints the model that served each turn, and the transcript under 
bench/results/
records it.

To compare whole conversations, 

bench/multiturn.py
runs an agentic loop over each coding task, with the project files in the first prompt and the test output fed back after every edit. It also runs four scripted chats of seven turns that alternate simple turns with design, debugging, and code-writing turns, and it replays the full history on every turn. Turns with a cheap check (expected text, a word limit, bullets, or assertions against the returned function) record whether the check passed. The design responses aren’t graded.

The 

--max-conv-cost
option (default 1 USD) caps each conversation, and 
--max-spend
stops the runner from starting new conversations. The summary shows, for each model group, the coding conversations that passed, the chat checks that passed, and the estimated cost per coding conversation, per chat, and in total.

The runners execute model-written Python on your machine. The subprocess that runs the tests has no credentials in its environment, but it isn’t an operating system sandbox: the code can read any file that your user can read and can reach the network. Use a disposable development environment with no long-lived AWS credentials on disk, and protect the files under 

bench/results/
, which contain prompts, model responses, tool output, and generated code.

Interpret your results

The sample’s tasks are small and illustrative. To decide whether routing fits your workload, replace or extend them with tasks that represent your own code base, and keep the following in mind as you read the runner’s output.

  • Start with SOLVED, then read COST/SOLVED – A group that solves fewer tasks can show a lower COST/TASK and still cost more per solved task, because failed runs add cost without adding solved tasks. Compare the routed group’s COST/SOLVED with each baseline group’s only after you’ve compared how many tasks each group solved.
  • Look at the hard tasks separately – Aggregate numbers can hide a single task that drives the result. Break results down by task. Stage decides from failures in the history, so it can’t route a hard task to the capable candidate in advance. An escalated turn also replays the whole failed attempt, which can make a recovery more expensive than a run that started on the capable candidate. If a few hard tasks dominate your cost, consider routing them to a dedicated model group, or choose an efficient candidate that solves more of them.
  • Run enough repeats – Model outputs vary from run to run. With only a handful of runs per group, a difference of one or two solved tasks can be noise. Increase 
    --repeats
    until the differences you care about are stable, and apply a statistical test, such as Fisher’s exact test for solve rates, before you act on a gap.
  • Account for the turn limit – A low 
    --max-turns
    value penalizes a model that explores before it edits, because it leaves fewer turns to repair a failing edit. Set the limit to match how your agents run in practice.
  • Account for output caps – If a group’s replies hit 
    max_tokens
    , the measured cost is a lower bound, and the shortened replies also shorten the history that later turns replay. Check the transcripts for truncated replies before you compare chat costs.
  • Treat costs as estimates – The runners estimate cost from token usage and the PRICES table, not from your bill. Prompt caching, batch inference, and pricing changes all affect your actual cost. Confirm with Amazon Bedrock pricing and your AWS Cost and Usage Reports.
  • Test the settings you plan to run – Results apply only to the models, profile settings, and tasks that you measured. If you change a candidate, the Stage settings, or switch to the Random profile, measure again.

Use these readings to choose among three options for each workload: the routed group, a single-model group, or a profile with different candidates or settings. Rerun the same measurement when you change models, prompts, or agent behavior.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the stack. The AWS CDK needs an 

allowedCidr
value to synthesize the app, but the value doesn’t matter here:

CloudFormation deletes the master key secret with no recovery window, so copy the key first if you need it. The gateway image stays in the AWS CDK bootstrap repository in Amazon ECR.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to deploy LiteLLM with the NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard routing plugin on AWS, configure Stage and Random routing across models on Amazon Bedrock, and measure cost per solved task for a routed model group alongside single-model baselines. Because the total cost of an agentic task depends on turns, history, and retries, price per token alone isn’t a reliable guide. Measuring cost per solved task on your own tasks gives you the evidence to choose a configuration.

To get started, deploy the sample repository in a development account, and measure Stage routing and single-model baselines on tasks from your own workload. To learn more, see the Switchyard LiteLLM plugin guide and the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Share your questions in the comments.

entries.title: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime V2 snapshots your initialized environment and restores it for each new session, so session start no longer grows with image size. This post explains how V2 starts a session, how to measure session start time, and four patterns to keep work off the first request.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime

Agents today review code, process claims, and run unattended for hours. Many also sit behind interactive experiences where a person waits for the first response. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime gives these agents a fully managed, serverless environment: each session runs in its own isolated microVM, the platform scales to zero when there’s no work, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume.

AgentCore runtime with 

platformVersion
set to “V2” changes how sessions start. Instead of initializing your container for every session, it prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores that snapshot for each new session. Session start times are faster and more consistent. V2 also reclaims memory your sessions don’t use, so your bill tracks what your agent uses.

For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes. Some agents need restructuring to get the full benefit, and for chat and voice experiences even 2 seconds is too slow. This post explains how V2 starts a session, how to measure session start time, and how to keep work off the first request, including build hooks, which AgentCore runtime now supports. We cover four patterns, from changes to your agent’s code to starting sessions before users need them.

Which pattern do you need?

Your situationWhat to doSection
A new session in about 2 seconds is fineSwitch to V2 and do all initialization before 
app.run()
 Keep work off the first request
Your agent needs large files, a CLI, or a browser early, and can’t hold them in its processAdd a build hook to load and prime them while the snapshot is builtWorking with hooks
You need sub-second, and users engage before they send their first request (opening the app or a chat window)Start the session in the background when the user engagesPre-warm on user engagement

How V2 starts a session

AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM. On V1, AgentCore pulls your container image from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), starts the container, and runs your initialization code before it can process the first request. The image pull dominates, so cold start grows with image size.

V2 does that work once. When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore runtime starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping (

GET /ping
), which must arrive within 120 seconds. It then clears the operating system’s file cache, to keep the snapshot small, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot.

This is a change from V1: Every create or update now takes a few minutes while the snapshot is built.

In this post, init means everything your agent does before 

/ping
reports healthy. With the AgentCore Python SDK, that’s everything before 
app.run()
. If you run your own HTTP server, in 
Node.js
or another language, report healthy only after your initialization finishes.

When a new session arrives, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM. Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with its imports, objects, and clients in place. Files from your image are loaded lazily: each block is fetched the first time a session reads it.

Three facts follow from these flows, and the rest of this post builds on them:

  • Memory comes back whole. Anything your process held at snapshot time, and anything in a RAM-backed file system such as 
    /dev/shm
    , is available at memory speed from the first access.
  • File reads don’t carry over. The file cache is cleared before the freeze, so reading a file during init doesn’t make it fast in a restored session.
  • Image files are fetched on first read. The first read of a block comes from snapshot storage and is then cached closer to the host.

The following table shows what that means for the work a typical agent does, depending on where it does it:

WorkDone during initDone in the handler
Import librariesIn memory when the session startsRead from the image in every new session
Create clients (for example, 
boto3
)		 Restored with endpoint and credential resolution done. Sockets reconnect on first useBuilt from scratch in every new session
Open network connectionsStale after the restore. Close them before the snapshotOpened fresh
Load static data from the image and keep it in an objectIn memory when the session startsRead from the image in every new session
Read a file from the image without keeping the dataNo effect, because the file cache is clearedRead from the image in every new session

If you know AWS Lambda SnapStart, this will feel familiar. Marc Brooker’s post on how SnapStart loads snapshots and the SnapStart priming strategies post are useful background.

Everything in the table assumes your agent can keep what it needs in its own process. That isn’t always possible. A CLI that runs as a separate process and exits, or a browser binary, is read during init and then gone, so a restored session fetches it from the image again. For these cases, you can add a build hook, covered in “Working with hooks.” Figure 3 shows where it runs.

Measure before you optimize

Latency in an agentic application isn’t one number. A request spends time in AgentCore runtime getting a session ready to run your code, then in your code: model calls, tool calls, sub-agents, and streaming the response back. You fix these in different ways, so start by finding out which one dominates.

AgentCore runtime publishes both as Amazon CloudWatch metrics in the 

AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore
namespace. 
Latency
is the time to first byte. 
OverheadLatency
is the part that belongs to the platform, such as starting the microVM and restoring the snapshot on a new session.
What you wantHow to get it
TTFB (Time to first byte)
Latency
Runtime time
OverheadLatency
Your code’s time
Latency
− 
OverheadLatency
Init timeMeasured in your code at startup (see the following example). It isn’t part of any request on V2

Init doesn’t appear in these metrics because on V2 it runs once, while the snapshot is built, and not in each session. It adds to how long a create or update takes to reach READY, not to request latency. To see how long it takes, log it once before 

app.run()
. The line appears in your runtime’s build logs:

How to read the split:

  • High 
    OverheadLatency
    on new sessions: the time is in session start. Use the patterns later in this post to start sessions before users need them.
  • Your code’s time is much higher on the first request than on the second in the same session: work that belongs in init is running in your handler. Add custom spans in AgentCore Observability (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore) around tool setup, file loads, and late imports to find it, then move it into init.

Report percentiles such as P90 and P99, or trimmed means such as TM90, which averages the fastest 90% of requests and drops the slowest tail. A plain average hides the slow requests. 

OverheadLatency
covers requests to running sessions as well as new ones, so its distribution depends on how many of your requests start a new session. Compare runs with a similar mix.

Test at the rate of new sessions you expect in production, not with a handful of sessions after a deploy.

To include network time from your client, measure on the client as well. Time the invoke call, have your handler return how long it ran, and subtract. Both timestamps come from the same machine, so clock differences between the client and the microVM don’t matter. If you stream, very small events can be held back until a few hundred bytes of output build up, so time to first event can read higher than session start.

Keep work off the first request

The usual cold start advice is to import lazily and keep initialization small. On V2, do the opposite: init runs once, when the snapshot is built, and work deferred to the handler is paid by every new session. This applies to static work: imports, clients, and data from your image. Dynamic data can’t be snapshotted. The next section covers it.

The agents that notice most are the ones that read large files from their image at request time: weights for a small local model, embeddings, datasets, large libraries, a browser binary for automation, or a CLI toolchain that a coding agent runs as subprocesses. Reading many small files, as compiling a TypeScript project does, has the same effect. An agent that imports a few libraries and calls a hosted model mostly needs to get its imports and clients right.

How to restructure your agent

Create objects during init, not only imports. Creating an object loads the modules it depends on and keeps them in active memory. Initialize local tools that use external libraries during init too, not when the agent first calls them.

Create your clients during init. Endpoint resolution, credential resolution, and the client’s modules all come back with the snapshot. Sockets don’t, but 

boto3
clients reconnect cleanly on the first call. Some other network clients first try the stale socket, which adds hundreds of milliseconds, so close their connections before the snapshot.

Keep static data in memory, such as prompts, skill front matter, configuration, and small indexes. Hold the data in an object, not only a read of it:

Keep tools running instead of starting them per request. A subprocess launched in the handler reads its binary and libraries from the image in every new session. A long-running helper started during init, such as a language server or a worker process with its imports done, comes back as part of process memory. Talk to it over a pipe or socket.

Copy files you can’t hold in memory to a RAM-backed disk. Toolchains like 

tsc
run as separate programs that read their own files. Copy them to 
/dev/shm
or a ramfs mount during init so their reads come from memory.

Ship compiled bytecode. 

uv pip install
doesn’t compile by default, so late imports also compile from source. Set 
UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1
or use 
pip install --compile
.

The example below builds the agent, its model, and its clients during init, so every session inherits them:

The trade-off: time to first byte on a new session is the time to start the microVM and restore the snapshot, plus the time your handler takes. Moving work into init shortens the handler, but anything you hold in memory makes the snapshot larger. You also pay for that held memory in every session. Measure end-to-end session start before and after the change, so you know you’ve reduced latency and not only moved it from the handler to the restore.

Reference card

DataApproach
Large files the first request needs, such as a model, a CLI, or a browserHold them in memory during init, or prime them with a build hook
Large reference data read selectivelyMount Amazon S3 Files or Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) during init, through an access point (requires virtual private cloud (VPC) mode)
Files the agent rarely readsLeave them on the image, or move them to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), S3 Files, or Amazon EFS
Files the session createsNo change needed

Working with hooks

A build hook builds on init and doesn’t replace it. Do what you can in init and use the hook for what init can’t cover. You expose an HTTP endpoint in your container, and AgentCore runtime sends it a 

POST
request twice while it builds your runtime:
  • Before the snapshot. On the build microVM, after your agent reports healthy and before the freeze. Anything your agent loads here and keeps in memory is part of the snapshot, so every session starts with it.
  • After a test restore. On a separate microVM that restores the snapshot to check it. Nothing from this call is snapshotted. Use it to read the files your sessions will need, which shapes what restored sessions fetch first.

The 

X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Warmup-Type
header tells your agent which call it’s handling: 
memory
for the first, 
disk
for the second. The two calls share 120 seconds, so the 
disk
call gets whatever time the 
memory
call leaves. Return a 
2xx
response only after the work is done. Any other response, a failed connection, or running out of time fails the create or update, and AgentCore runtime doesn’t retry. The 
build-logs-
streams in your runtime’s log group show which call failed and why.

Hooks are available on V2 runtimes. Configure them with 

hooksConfiguration
when you create or update the runtime:

The port is optional and defaults to your agent’s serving port. If you set it, use a port from 8000 to 12000 that isn’t reserved by the platform. The path can’t match a route AgentCore runtime already uses on that port, such as 

POST /invocations
or 
GET /ping
. 
UpdateAgentRuntime
replaces the whole hook configuration, so include 
hooksConfiguration
in every update where you want to keep the hook.

In the agent, handle both call types on the same endpoint:

For the full configuration reference, see Configure lifecycle hooks for AgentCore runtime. For a complete code example, see the sample code.

Snapshot pitfalls: What must stay in the handler

Everything created during init is frozen into the snapshot until your next deploy, and every session starts with the same copy. For most objects that’s the point. For the values below, it’s a bug, and for random values, a security issue.

Load dynamic data in the handler, once per session. Tool catalogs from AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), feature flags, and price lists change after you deploy. Load them in the handler and cache them at module level, so each session fetches them once. Sessions can last up to 8 hours, so give the cache an expiry:

Call 

get_tools()
from the handler and pass the result to the agent you created during init.

Create per-session values in the handler.

ValueWhere to create itWhy
Random values, nonces, secrets, keysIn the handler, with 
secrets
, 
os.urandom()
, or 
uuid.uuid4()
 Library random state (Python’s 
random
, NumPy) created during init is identical in every session. Values from the operating system are unique
Current and elapsed timeIn the handler, with 
time.time()
 An init timestamp is fixed at snapshot time, and 
time.monotonic()
doesn’t count the time the snapshot spent stored
Timers, rate limiters, TTL cachesUse wall-clock time, or reset them on the first requestAnything measuring elapsed time with a monotonic clock sees almost no gap across the restore
Credentials and tokens you fetch yourselfRefresh them when they expireValues loaded during init can expire before a session starts

Know the limits. A session ends when its idle timeout expires (

idleRuntimeSessionTimeout
: 15 minutes by default, from 60 seconds up to 8 hours), when it reaches its maximum lifetime (
maxLifetime
: 8 hours by default and at most), or when you stop it.

Sub-second: Start the session before the user needs it

Suppose your new session takes about 2 seconds to start, including all the timing breakdown covered in the preceding sections. A session that’s already running answers in about 200 ms. For a chat or voice experience, the way to sub-second is to make sure the session has started before the user’s first request arrives. There are two ways to do that.

Pre-warm on user engagement

Most interactive applications get a signal before the first prompt: the user opens the app, a chat window, or a support page. Use it. Generate a session ID, send the agent a warm-up request in the background, and keep the session ID with the conversation. By the time the user has typed their first message, the session is running.

This pattern needs no extra infrastructure and fully hides session start whenever users take more than about 2 seconds to send their first message. It costs a session for each user who engages but never sends a prompt. A short idle timeout keeps that small.

Conclusion

On V2, AgentCore runtime moves most of the work of starting a session to deployment time. Your container starts once, and every new session restores the result: memory comes back whole, and files are fetched on first read.

To keep session startup time near 2 seconds, do your static work during init, hold the data the first request needs in memory, and keep dynamic and per-session values in the handler. For files your process can’t hold, add a build hook. To get under a second, start the session before the user needs it: on user engagement when you get a signal.

To get started, set 

platformVersion
to V2 when you create or update a runtime, then review Optimize your agent for AgentCore runtime V2. For questions about your workload, reach out to your AWS account team.

entries.title: OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures
entries.summary: Deploy OpenFold3-preview from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to predict 3D structures of proteins, DNA, RNA, and ligand complexes in your own AWS account. The post covers asynchronous inference, multi-GPU parallelism, bringing your own MSAs for accuracy and privacy, and scaling to zero to reduce cost.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures

You can deploy OpenFold3-preview from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. The OpenFold Consortium and the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University developed OpenFold3 as an open source biomolecular structure prediction model. With a few lines of code, you can typically deploy OpenFold3 into your own AWS account. You can then predict the 3D structures of proteins, DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, and the complexes they form. The endpoint runs with network isolation, which you can use to help keep your sequences within your AWS account.

Computational drug discovery teams now use structure prediction as a core part of their work. Teams use it in target identification, antibody and protein engineering, and structure-based virtual screening. Teams have found running these models challenging. You need GPU infrastructure, a working CUDA and PyTorch stack, large model checkpoints, and a serving layer that handles requests that take minutes rather than milliseconds. SageMaker JumpStart can handle much of that work for you. OpenFold3 runs in an AWS-maintained container on a managed Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint. The endpoint is designed to handle request queuing and GPU warmup, and you can add autoscaling.

In this post, we show you how to:

  • Deploy OpenFold3-preview on a SageMaker asynchronous inference endpoint.
  • Submit structure prediction jobs and interpret the results, including predicted structures and confidence scores.
  • Run several predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances.
  • Supply your own multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to improve prediction accuracy while helping keep your sequences private.
  • Help reduce costs by scaling your endpoint to zero when it’s idle.

Overview of OpenFold3

OpenFold3 is an all-atom structure prediction model. It predicts the joint 3D structure of a set of molecules from their sequences. It isn’t limited to single protein chains: It can fold multi-chain protein complexes, protein–nucleic acid assemblies, and protein–ligand complexes in one prediction.

AttributeDetails
DeveloperOpenFold Consortium / AlQuraishi Lab, Columbia University
Model typeAll-atom biomolecular structure prediction
InputsProtein, DNA, and RNA sequences. Small-molecule ligands as SMILES
OutputsPredicted structures in mmCIF format, with confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, PDE)
VersionOpenFold3 0.4.1, 
of3-p2-155k
checkpoint
LicenseApache 2.0
JumpStart model ID
huggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3
Supported instances
ml.g6.2xlarge
, 
ml.g6.4xlarge
(default), 
ml.g6.12xlarge

The OpenFold3 developers release its code and model weights under the Apache 2.0 license, and they publish the training data and methods. Research organizations and pharmaceutical companies can inspect the model, fine-tune it, and build on it under the terms of that license. The developers describe OpenFold3-preview as a research preview.

Use cases

  • Target and complex structure prediction – Predict structures for targets that have no experimental structure, including multi-chain assemblies and protein–nucleic acid complexes.
  • Protein–ligand co-folding – Fold a protein together with a small molecule supplied as SMILES to generate binding-pose hypotheses for structure-based design.
  • Antibody and protein engineering – Evaluate designed variants by predicting their structures and comparing confidence across candidates.
  • High-throughput screening pipelines – Queue large batches of prediction jobs against an autoscaling endpoint and process the results directly from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).

Why OpenFold3 uses asynchronous inference

Most JumpStart models, such as large language models and embedding models, deploy to real-time endpoints. A real-time endpoint returns its response within a single request, and that request is capped at 60 seconds. Structure prediction works differently. Folding time grows with the number and length of the chains in a query, and real-world proteins and complexes often take several minutes.

For this reason, OpenFold3 on JumpStart runs on SageMaker Asynchronous Inference:

  • You upload the request to Amazon S3 and call 
    InvokeEndpointAsync
    , which returns immediately.
  • The endpoint queues the request and processes it, with an invocation timeout of up to 1 hour.
  • The endpoint writes the result, or the error details, to an S3 location you choose. You can poll for it or get a notification through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS).

Two properties of asynchronous endpoints suit scientific workloads especially well. First, they queue bursts of requests internally, so you can submit a large batch of sequences without building your own job queue. Second, they can scale to zero instances when the queue is empty, which helps you avoid paying for idle instances between experiments.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need:

  • An AWS account, and a SageMaker AI execution role for the endpoint. Following least privilege, this AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role needs read and write access only to the S3 prefix that you use for requests and results. For more information, see How to use SageMaker AI execution roles.
  • IAM permissions for the identity that runs the code: to create, describe, invoke, and delete the model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, plus 
    iam:PassRole
    for the execution role. For the optional scale-to-zero section, it also needs AWS Application Auto Scaling and Amazon CloudWatch alarm permissions. In production, scope these permissions to your resources rather than using broad managed policies such as 
    AmazonSageMakerFullAccess
    . For more information, see Complete the prerequisites for asynchronous inference.
  • Access to Amazon SageMaker Studio, a SageMaker notebook instance, or a local IDE.
  • The SageMaker Python SDK v3 and py3Dmol, which you can install with 
    pip install "sagemaker>=3,<4" py3Dmol
    .
  • Service quota for at least one 
    ml.g6.4xlarge
    endpoint instance in your AWS Region. You also need quota for 
    ml.g6.12xlarge
    if you follow the multi-GPU section. You can check your quotas and request increases in the Service Quotas console under Amazon SageMaker.

Important: SageMaker endpoints are billed per instance-hour while they’re running, including while they’re idle. To avoid unexpected charges, follow the Clean up section, or configure scale-to-zero as described later in this post. For pricing details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.

Discover OpenFold3 in SageMaker JumpStart

  • Open SageMaker Studio and choose JumpStart in the navigation pane.
  • Search for OpenFold3.
  • Open the model card to review the model description, license, and supported instance types.
  • Open the example notebook from the model card. It contains the complete asynchronous deployment walkthrough shown in this post.

Deploy OpenFold3 with the SageMaker Python SDK

First, build the model from its JumpStart configuration and define an 

AsyncInferenceConfig
. The output and failure paths are the S3 locations where the endpoint writes results and error details.

Setting 

accept_eula=True
confirms that you’ve reviewed and accepted the model’s license terms, which is required to deploy this model. If you run this code outside SageMaker Studio, also pass your SageMaker execution role to 
ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config
with 
role_arn=""
.

The endpoint stores your requests and results in Amazon S3, and they contain your sequences and predicted structures. For proprietary sequences, consider using a dedicated S3 bucket or prefix with server-side encryption using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key that you manage. To encrypt results with your key, pass its ARN to 

AsyncInferenceConfig
as 
kms_key_id
. Restrict access with a bucket policy that allows only the roles that run this workflow, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule to expire request and result objects that you don’t need to keep. For more information, see Security best practices for Amazon S3.

Deployment typically completes within minutes. This includes a warmup step in which the container runs a short prediction on each GPU, so that the GPUs are warmed up when the endpoint reaches 

InService
.

Tip: G6 capacity can be limited in some Regions. If a deployment fails with 

InsufficientInstanceCapacity
, retry later, choose a different supported instance size, or deploy in another AWS Region where the model is available.

Run a structure prediction

A request is a JSON document with one or more named queries, and each query lists its chains. All chains in a query are folded together as one complex. Separate queries are folded independently.

Each chain has these fields:

  • molecule_type
    – 
    protein
    , 
    dna
    , 
    rna
    , or 
    ligand
    .
  • chain_ids
    – a list of chain identifiers, such as 
    ["A"]
    . To specify identical copies, such as a homodimer, use 
    ["A", "B"]
    .
  • sequence
    – the residue sequence, for protein, DNA, and RNA chains.
  • smiles
    – a SMILES string, used for ligand chains instead of 
    sequence
    .

The following example folds human ubiquitin, a well-characterized 76-residue protein:

Then poll S3 for either the result or a failure record:

A request with invalid input, such as a malformed chain or an unsupported MSA name, still produces a result object, but with 

"status": "error"
and an 
error
message instead of structures. The last check surfaces that message.

Prediction time grows with the size of the input. In our tests on ml.g6.4xlarge, smaller proteins completed more quickly than larger proteins.

Interpret the results

The response contains a 

status
, a list of predicted 
structures
in mmCIF format, and their matching 
confidences
. By default, OpenFold3 generates five diffusion samples per query, so each query returns five candidate structures. Each sample comes with two confidence files: a detailed one (
*_confidences.json
) and a summary (
*_confidences_aggregated.json
). The summary includes a 
sample_ranking_score
that you can use to pick the best sample.

You can open the 

.cif
files in any structure viewer, such as PyMOL, ChimeraX, or Mol*. To view a structure inline in a notebook, use 
py3Dmol
:

The prediction shows ubiquitin’s compact fold: a mixed beta-sheet packed against a single alpha-helix. Most of the structure is blue (high confidence). Only the flexible C-terminal tail, at the top of the image, shifts toward yellow and red, which matches the tail’s known flexibility in experimental structures.

The confidence metrics tell you how much to trust each prediction:

  • pLDDT (predicted local distance difference test) – Per-atom confidence in the local structure, on a scale of 0–100. Higher is better, and values above about 70 generally indicate a reliable local structure. The summary file reports the average as 
    avg_plddt
    .
  • pTM and ipTM (predicted TM-score and interface pTM) – Overall confidence in the fold, and in how chains and ligands are positioned relative to each other, on a scale of 0–1. For complexes, ipTM is the key number. The summary file also reports 
    chain_pair_iptm
    for each pair of chains.
  • PAE (predicted aligned error) and PDE (predicted distance error) – Per-residue-pair error estimates, in the detailed confidence file. Use them to judge the relative placement of domains and chains.

Fold a complex

To predict a complex, list several chains in the same query. The following example co-folds human carbonic anhydrase II with its catalytic zinc ion and the drug acetazolamide. This is a well-studied complex with experimental structures in the Protein Data Bank (for example, PDB 3HS4):

Protein sequences in these examples are from UniProt (P0CG48, P00918). You submit and read this request the same way as the ubiquitin example. For complexes like this one, prediction quality depends heavily on providing an MSA, as the next sections show.

Run predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances

A single OpenFold3 prediction runs on one GPU, so a multi-GPU instance doesn’t make an individual prediction faster. Instead, you can run several predictions at once. On a multi-GPU instance such as 

ml.g6.12xlarge
, which has four GPUs, the container assigns each concurrent request its own GPU. To use all the GPUs, set 
max_concurrent_invocations_per_instance
to the number of GPUs on the instance (four, for 
ml.g6.12xlarge
):

This creates a second endpoint, so remember to delete it as well when you’re done (see Clean up).

In our tests, four concurrent predictions each ran on a separate GPU, with throughput gains that grew with protein size. For larger proteins, the cost per prediction that we measured on 

ml.g6.12xlarge
, based on On-Demand instance pricing, was close to that of 
ml.g6.4xlarge
. Your results depend on your inputs and Region. For pricing, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.

Note: 

ml.g6.12xlarge
capacity can be limited. If it isn’t available in your Region, you can increase throughput by scaling out across several 
ml.g6.4xlarge
instances with the autoscaling configuration described later in this post.

Use the following table to choose an instance:

WorkloadRecommended instanceWhy
Interactive exploration by a single user
ml.g6.2xlarge
or 
ml.g6.4xlarge
 One GPU handles one prediction at a time at the lowest hourly cost of the supported instances
Team use or bursts of concurrent requests
ml.g6.12xlarge
with 
max_concurrent_invocations_per_instance=4
 Four predictions run in parallel instead of queuing
High-throughput screening
ml.g6.12xlarge
with autoscaling		 Highest throughput per instance of the supported instances. Scales out with queue depth and back to zero

Improve prediction accuracy with your own MSAs

OpenFold3 can take a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) as an additional input for each protein chain. An MSA is a set of evolutionarily related sequences aligned to your query. Co-variation across those sequences signals which residues are likely to be in contact, so MSAs can substantially improve accuracy for many proteins and complexes.

To help keep your sequences within your AWS account, the JumpStart endpoint runs with network isolation and doesn’t call external MSA servers. Instead, it accepts precomputed MSAs in the request. You generate alignments with the pipeline and sequence databases you already use, on infrastructure you control, and pass them to the endpoint. This design can help drug discovery programs that need to keep proprietary sequences private.

If you don’t supply an MSA, the endpoint predicts from the sequence alone. That can work well for small, well-characterized proteins such as ubiquitin. For most real-world targets and complexes, include an MSA. The rest of this section shows how, and how much it improves results.

Bring your own MSA

Each protein chain accepts a 

precomputed_msa
field: a list of alignments, each with a 
name
and the alignment 
content
in A3M or Stockholm format. For a single merged alignment, such as the output of a ColabFold MMseqs2 search, use the name 
colabfold_main
:

This example has one protein chain. If a query has several different protein chains, compute an MSA for each one and attach it to that chain’s 

precomputed_msa
field. Identical copies listed together under one 
chain_ids
entry, such as a homodimer, share a single MSA.

The endpoint also accepts other alignment names, such as 

uniref90_hits
, 
mgnify_hits
, and 
bfd_uniclust_hits
, if you generate MSAs with a different pipeline. Because the request is staged in S3, you can send large alignments. In our tests, alignments of several megabytes worked.

You can generate MSAs with tools such as ColabFold (MMseqs2) or HHblits or JackHMMER. To help keep proprietary sequences inside your environment, run the search on your own AWS infrastructure against locally hosted sequence databases, rather than sending sequences to a public server. For example, ColabFold’s 

colabfold_batch
command uses the public ColabFold MSA server by default, so for proprietary sequences, use 
colabfold_search
with locally hosted databases instead.

How much difference does an MSA make?

We folded the carbonic anhydrase II, zinc, and acetazolamide complex from the previous section twice on the same endpoint: once in single-sequence mode, and once with an MSA from a ColabFold MMseqs2 search.

Metric (first of 5 samples)Without MSAWith MSA
Average pLDDT3098
pTM0.220.98
ipTM0.490.98
Zinc–His94/His96/His119 distance2.3–9.4 Å2.0 Å each
Acetazolamide nitrogen–zinc distance5.6 Å2.0 Å
Prediction time~1.5 minutes~1.5 minutes

With the MSA, OpenFold3 recovers the known binding mode. The zinc ion is coordinated by the three active-site histidines, and the acetazolamide sulfonamide nitrogen binds directly to the zinc, matching the experimental structure. Without the MSA, the protein fold has low confidence and the binding site isn’t formed. Adding the MSA didn’t noticeably change prediction time.

Superimposed on the crystal structure, the MSA-based prediction matches it closely: the protein backbone deviates by 0.2 Å (Cα RMSD), the zinc ion by less than 0.1 Å, and the acetazolamide heavy atoms by 0.4 Å RMSD. The single-sequence prediction is misfolded, with a Cα RMSD of 22 Å.

Carbonic anhydrase II with acetazolamide is one of the most extensively studied complexes in the Protein Data Bank, and closely related structures are likely part of OpenFold3’s training data. Treat this example as a demonstration of the workflow and of how much an MSA matters, not as a benchmark of accuracy on novel targets.

When you compare OpenFold3 results against other tools or published benchmarks, compare like with like: single-sequence results with single-sequence results, and MSA-based results with MSA-based results.

Help reduce cost: Scale to zero when idle

Asynchronous endpoints can scale down to zero instances when no requests are queued, and scale back up when new requests arrive. This pattern suits structure prediction work, which often runs in bursts.

Target tracking scales the endpoint down to zero after the queue has been empty for a while. In our tests, that took about 15–20 minutes. However, target tracking doesn’t scale the endpoint back up from zero. To start an instance when a request arrives and no instances are running, add a step-scaling policy that’s triggered by the 

HasBacklogWithoutCapacity
metric:

When a request arrives at an endpoint with zero instances, it waits in the queue while an instance starts. The first request after scaling from zero will take longer to complete as it includes time for the alarm to trigger, the instance to start, plus the prediction itself. Later requests in the same burst run at normal speed. This trade-off can work well for batch workloads. For interactive use, set 

MinCapacity=1
to keep one instance warm. For more details, see Autoscale an asynchronous endpoint.

Clean up

To stop incurring charges, delete the resources you created when you’re finished. If you configured autoscaling, remove it first: delete the Amazon CloudWatch alarm, then deregister the scalable target. Then delete each endpoint, its endpoint configuration, and its model, including the multi-GPU endpoint if you deployed it:

If you no longer need the request and result objects, you can also delete them from 

s3:///openfold3-async/
.

Conclusion

With OpenFold3 on SageMaker JumpStart, research and drug discovery teams can deploy an open, inspectable structure prediction model into their own AWS account with a few lines of code. Asynchronous inference handles long-running folds and bursty batch workloads, and multi-GPU instances run predictions in parallel. Network isolation helps you keep proprietary sequences private, and because you can bring your own MSAs, you can benefit from MSAs without sending sequences to an external server. With scale-to-zero, you stop paying for endpoint instances after the queue has been empty long enough for the endpoint to scale in. Other charges, such as for Amazon S3 storage, still apply.

The code in this post is sample code for experimentation. Before you use it with proprietary or regulated data, work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements.

To get started, search for OpenFold3 in SageMaker JumpStart, or open the example notebook from the model card. To learn more about the features used in this post, see Asynchronous inference and Autoscale an asynchronous endpoint. To discuss your structural biology workloads, contact your AWS account team.

entries.title: Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot
entries.summary: Learn how AssemblyAI runs cost-optimized speech-to-text inference at scale on AWS, using Amazon ECS, Amazon EC2 Spot GPU instances, and an Amazon SQS-based retry architecture to achieve 70% cost savings while maintaining SLA commitments across European Regions.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot

Speech-to-text inference is computationally intensive. Each audio file triggers a pipeline of deep learning models (acoustic models, language models, and post-processing stages) running on NVIDIA GPUs to meet latency requirements. At scale, this means thousands of GPU instances running continuously.

AssemblyAI needed a way to run GPU-intensive inference workloads cost-effectively at scale, without sacrificing the availability and latency guarantees their customers depend on. Running entirely on On-Demand Instances would be cost-prohibitive. Spot Instances offer significant savings, while Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. AssemblyAI needed an architecture that absorbs Spot interruptions gracefully while maintaining service level agreement (SLA) commitments. Additionally, customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, finance, and legal, must keep audio data within specific geographic boundaries. They implement strict data residency configurations in European AWS Regions.

Available on AWS Marketplace, AssemblyAI provides an API for transcription, speaker detection, sentiment analysis, chapter detection, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction. Their models transcribe and analyze speech for high-volume workloads across industries including technology, media, healthcare, and financial services.

In this post, we show you how AssemblyAI runs cost-optimized AI inference at scale for their speech-to-text platform. The architecture uses Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Spot Instances, and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Together, these services combine a flexible fleet of NVIDIA GPUs, ECS capacity providers, and a queue-based retry mechanism. The result is significant cost savings while maintaining SLA commitments across European AWS Regions.

Solution overview

AssemblyAI’s inference platform runs on Amazon ECS with compute capacity managed through ECS capacity providers. The fleet mixes Amazon EC2 Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances across multiple NVIDIA GPU instance families, running a single inference model per GPU at a scale of thousands of instances. The architecture is built on four pillars that work together to deliver cost-optimized and resilient inference:

  • Amazon ECS capacity providers mixing Spot and On-Demand.
  • Multi-family GPU Spot diversification across EC2 instance types (such as g4dn.xlarge, g4dn.2xlarge, g5.xlarge, g5.4xlarge, and g6.2xlarge).
  • Queue-based retry architecture using Amazon SQS for interruption recovery.
  • Regional deployment across US West (Oregon) us-west-2 and Europe (London) eu-west-2 for data residency compliance.

The following diagram illustrates how this solution is deployed:

An Amazon ECS cluster runs within a virtual private cloud (VPC) across multiple Availability Zones. The cluster hosts GPU-backed ECS tasks (shown as ECS Task, GPU Spot 1 and ECS Task GPU Spot 2) that poll the queue and process inference jobs. Each task retrieves audio files from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and writes the completed transcription to a results store, which AssemblyAI configures to deliver the output to the end customer.

When a Spot Instance receives an interruption notice, Amazon EventBridge invokes the Spot Interruption Handler (an AWS Lambda function). The handler returns the in-flight job to the Main Job SQS Queue so another healthy ECS task can pick it up. Customers configure their system to route jobs that exhaust retry attempts to a Dead Letter SQS Queue for investigation. Amazon CloudWatch Metrics monitors the health of the fleet and the Spot interruption events, providing observability across the system.

Amazon ECS capacity providers and Spot diversification

To optimize inference costs without compromising reliability, AssemblyAI configures multiple capacity providers in a single capacity provider strategy within each ECS cluster. An On-Demand capacity provider serves as an always-on baseline, and a Spot capacity provider spans different GPU instance families and Availability Zones to serve spikes of demand. Each capacity provider associates with an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Amazon ECS managed scaling automates the scaling of GPU instances based on the capacity provider weights and the pending inference tasks. When the task queue grows, the Spot capacity provider requests additional instances from the diversified pool. When demand drops, instances scale in gracefully.

One of the most effective Spot best practices is to be flexible across a wide range of instance types to increase the chances of getting the aggregate compute capacity needed. Rather than depending on a single GPU instance family, AssemblyAI’s infrastructure spans three Amazon EC2 GPU instance families:

  • g4dn instances – Powered by NVIDIA T4 GPUs, providing a cost-effective baseline for standard speech recognition models.
  • g5 instances – Equipped with NVIDIA A10G GPUs, delivering higher throughput for more demanding model architectures.
  • g6 instances – Featuring NVIDIA L4 GPUs, offering improved performance-per-dollar for larger models including large language model-based inference.

By spreading demand across instance families and sizes, AssemblyAI draws from a significantly larger pool of available Spot capacity. Using the price-capacity optimized allocation strategy, Amazon EC2 provisions instances from the Spot capacity pools with the highest available capacity at the lowest price, reducing the likelihood of interruptions.

Queue-based retry for interruption resilience

Maintaining quality of service during Spot interruptions was a core design requirement. AssemblyAI decouples job submission from execution using Amazon SQS. When a transcription request arrives, it’s placed into an Amazon SQS queue. Amazon ECS tasks running on GPU instances poll the queue, pull jobs, and execute the inference pipeline. Individual jobs typically take between 15 seconds and several minutes depending on audio length.

When a Spot Instance receives a 2-minute interruption notice, the retry flow works as follows:

  • In-flight jobs that can complete within the 2-minute window finish normally. Jobs that need more time are returned to the Amazon SQS queue, where they become immediately available for other workers.
  • Another healthy GPU instance picks up the message, potentially on a different instance type or in a different Availability Zone, and completes the inference.

To reduce recovery time, AssemblyAI creates custom Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) containing model artifacts and container images in approximately 2 minutes. For end customers, the impact of a Spot interruption is a small increase in processing time, but the transcription completes successfully and is delivered as expected.

Regional deployment for data residency

Running in multiple AWS Regions allows AssemblyAI to support customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, financial services, and legal services, where audio data must never leave specific geographic boundaries. Each AWS Region runs a fully independent copy of the inference architecture: its own Amazon SQS queues, Amazon ECS clusters, capacity providers, and GPU fleets. Multiple GPU instance families (g4dn, g5, g6) are available in these European Regions with competitive Spot pricing. This instance diversity supports a reliable Spot-based inference service while meeting strict data residency requirements.

Results

By running Amazon EC2 Spot Instances with GPUs in production, AssemblyAI achieved 70 percent cost savings on inference compute compared to On-Demand pricing. As the platform grew nearly 4x year-over-year in compute demand, the Spot-based architecture kept unit economics sustainable. Operating at this scale, AssemblyAI learned that diversifying across instance families and sizes is the most effective lever for minimizing Spot interruption rates. The g4dn, g5, and g6 families tap into independent capacity pools, so when one family experiences capacity pressure, the others remain available. Designing fault tolerance from day one with queue-based retries and fast warm-up turns Spot interruptions into routine events while maintaining SLA commitments.

Conclusion

Teams running batch or near real-time AI workloads with similar characteristics (short-lived, independently retriable jobs on GPU compute) can apply this pattern. Start by diversifying instance families and building queue-based fault tolerance to take advantage of cost-effective Spot infrastructure without compromising availability.

To get started with GPU tasks on Amazon ECS, see Amazon ECS for GPU workloads. To evaluate Spot availability for your workload, explore using Spot placement scores for accelerated compute and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances best practices. AssemblyAI’s Speech-to-Text API is available on AWS Marketplace. To learn more about their platform, visit assemblyai.com.

entries.title: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock provides built-in, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it. This post shows how to attribute per-user Bedrock costs for AI developer and productivity tools using IAM Identity Center, session tags, and CUR 2.0, and how to enforce per-user usage limits.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock provides built-in, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it. The identity flows along with organizational tags, into AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) and AWS Cost Explorer while keeping data inside the AWS security boundary. This post shows you how to use these capabilities to answer three questions that every FinOps and AI Platform leader asks as AI tool adoption scales: What is the real per-user cost? Which teams generate the most spend, and does that spend correlate with the value they deliver? How should next year’s budget scale with headcount and adoption?

The approach works identically regardless of which AI coding or productivity tool makes the call. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode all invoke Amazon Bedrock through one of two inference endpoints: 

bedrock-runtime
or 
bedrock-mantle
, and Bedrock’s attribution mechanism operates at the endpoint layer, beneath any tool-specific logic. You configure identity propagation once, and every tool that routes inference through Bedrock inherits per-user cost visibility automatically.

By the end of this post, you will have AWS IAM Identity Center configured with your external identity provider for per-user attribution, session tags (team, cost center) flowing into CUR 2.0, Amazon Athena queries and dashboard options for ongoing cost visibility, and a clear understanding of Bedrock-native usage controls to enforce spending limits.

How Amazon Bedrock attribution works

Amazon Bedrock records the IAM identity of every inference caller with no changes required to your API calls. When a user invokes a model through either the 

bedrock-runtime
or 
bedrock-mantle
endpoint, Bedrock captures the caller’s full IAM ARN, including the session name for federated users and publishes it to CUR 2.0 in the 
line_item_iam_principal
column. In billing data, usage is aggregated per principal and per usage type for each export interval: one hour in an hourly export, one day in a daily export. CUR does not contain per-request cost. For per-prompt detail, use model invocation logs or request metadata tagging.

Optionally, you can attach tags to IAM principals or pass session tags during federation to add organizational dimensions. These tags appear in CUR 2.0 with the 

iamPrincipal/
prefix and in Cost Explorer as filterable dimensions. The mechanism supports four access patterns: IAM users, per-application roles, federated identities, and large language model (LLM) gateways proxying to Bedrock. For a comparison of all four, see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock. This post follows the federated identity pattern, which is the natural fit for AI coding and productivity tools where each developer or knowledge worker authenticates individually.

Amazon Bedrock offers additional attribution mechanisms beyond IAM principal tracking that organizations can layer depending on their needs (see Appendix A for a comparison). With Application Inference Profiles, you can tag spend by workload on the 

bedrock-runtime
endpoint. With Projects and Workspaces, you can isolate and tag spend on the 
bedrock-mantle
endpoint. Per-request metadata tagging provides per-prompt token-level detail in model invocation logs for workloads that need granularity finer than finer than CUR 2.0’s per-usage-type aggregation per export interval. You can combine these, for example, IAM principal attribution for per-user dollars on your invoice alongside per-request metadata tags for per-prompt detail in logs. The choice depends on your goal (see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock).

The attribution problem

The developer and productivity tools run on each user’s machine and call Amazon Bedrock directly, or through an LLM gateway. Users authenticate by assuming a shared IAM role, so every API call appears as 

assumed-role//
in billing. If every user assumes the role with the same fixed session name, or calls go through a gateway’s own role, CUR aggregates spend to a single principal. With IAM Identity Center, the session name is the user’s sign-in name, so each user gets their own principal. You can further enrich it with session tags (team, cost center, project). These fields flow into CUR 2.0’s 
line_item_iam_principal
column and cost allocation tags with the 
iamPrincipal/
prefix, making per-user spend queryable alongside the dollars, with zero changes to your Bedrock API calls.

Claude Platform on AWS and Claude for Enterprise route inference through Anthropic-managed infrastructure. For Claude Platform on AWS, usage is visible by workspace and API key in Anthropic’s admin console, and workspace tags flow to AWS billing. For Claude for Enterprise, per-user usage is visible in Anthropic’s admin console and Usage and Cost API. Spend limits are enforced natively by Anthropic.

Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have:

  • An AWS account with IAM permissions to access Bedrock models you intend to use.
  • AWS IAM Identity Center enabled in your management account.
  • An external identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity) with SCIM provisioning capability.
  • AWS CLI v2 configured on developer machines.
  • AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0) enabled with IAM principal data and delivered to an S3 bucket.
  • Cost allocation tags activated from the management (payer) account.
  • An Athena table configured to query CUR 2.0 data (see the GitHub sample to get started).

Step 1: Configure IAM Identity Center with your external IdP

Configure your external identity provider as the identity source in AWS IAM Identity Center. Navigate to IAM Identity Center → Settings → Identity source → Change identity source. Select “External identity provider” and configure SAML 2.0 or SCIM connectivity with your IdP. Enable SCIM provisioning to automatically synchronize users and groups, including organizational attributes like team and department.

Configure attribute mapping for session tags by navigating to Settings → Attributes for access control. Map your IdP’s organizational attributes to session tags that will flow into CUR 2.0. These attributes propagate as session tags (

aws:PrincipalTag/Team
, 
aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter
) on every API call the user makes, including every Bedrock invocation through both the 
bedrock-runtime
and 
bedrock-mantle
endpoints.

Step 2: Create a permission set for Bedrock access

Create a permission set in Identity Center that grants Bedrock invocation access. Each user gets their own session within this permission set. This is the foundation of per-user attribution. The specific IAM actions depend on which Bedrock endpoint the tool calls.

Tools that call the 

bedrock-mantle
endpoint (such as Codex and ChatGPT Work) require 
bedrock-mantle:CreateInference
and related actions scoped to a Project resource. Tools that call the 
bedrock-runtime
endpoint (such as Claude Code and Claude Desktop) require 
bedrock:InvokeModel
and 
bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream
scoped to the relevant foundation model or inference profile ARNs. You can combine both in a single permission set if your organization uses tools across both endpoints.
